questions.question: A charge of $0.7$ C is moving at an angle of $38^\circ$ to the vertical across magnetic field lines of strength $0.006$ T that are directed vertically down, at a velocity of $6.2$ m s$^{-1}$. Ignoring any effects due to gravitational fields, the shape of the path that the charge would follow as it moves through this magnetic field would be:
questions.answer: The velocity has a component perpendicular to $\mathbf B$ (which gives circular motion) and a component parallel to $\mathbf B$ (which is unaffected by the field and gives constant drift along the field lines). Together they give a helix (C).

questions.question: A charge of $0.7$ C is moving at an angle of $38^\circ$ to the vertical across magnetic field lines of strength $0.006$ T that are directed vertically down, at a velocity of $6.2$ m s$^{-1}$. Ignoring any effects due to gravitational fields, the magnitude of the force that the charge would experience as it passes through this magnetic field would be:
questions.answer: Only the component of velocity perpendicular to the field matters: $F=qvB\sin\theta=0.7\times6.2\times0.006\times\sin38^\circ=0.016$ N (B).

questions.question: A charge of $0.7$ C is moving at an angle of $38^\circ$ to the vertical across magnetic field lines of strength $0.006$ T that are directed vertically down, at a velocity of $6.2$ m s$^{-1}$. Ignoring any effects due to gravitational fields, the magnitude of the vertical displacement that the charge would have travelled through after a time of $6$ seconds would be:
questions.answer: The vertical component of velocity is parallel to the (vertical) field, so it is unchanged: $v_\parallel=6.2\cos38^\circ=4.89$ m s$^{-1}$. Over $6$ s the vertical displacement is $4.89\times6=29.3$ m (D).

questions.question: A particle with a charge of $+0.6$ mC is moving vertically downward through free space with a velocity of $200$ m s$^{-1}$ when it encounters a uniform electric field of strength $20$ N C$^{-1}$ directed vertically downward. After the charge has moved through a distance of $15$ metres in a direction parallel to the field, the magnitude of the amount of work done on the charge would be:

A particle with a charge of $+0.6$ mC is moving vertically downward through free space with a velocity of $200$ m s$^{-1}$ when it encounters a uniform electric field of strength $20$ N C$^{-1}$ directed vertically downward. If the mass of the charge was $3$ grams, the magnitude of the change in velocity of the charge over this $15$ metre distance would be closest to:

A particle with a charge of $+0.6$ mC is moving vertically downward through free space with a velocity of $200$ m s$^{-1}$ when it encounters a uniform electric field of strength $20$ N C$^{-1}$ directed vertically downward. The mass of the particle is $3$ grams. If the electric field was now set up horizontally instead of vertically, the magnitude of the displacement of the particle $4$ seconds from the instant the particle entered the field would be closest to:
questions.answer:
The $200$ m s$^{-1}$ vertical velocity is unaffected, so the vertical displacement is $200\times4=800$ m. The field gives a horizontal acceleration $a=\frac{qE}m=4$ m s$^{-2}$, so the horizontal displacement is $\frac12(4)(4)^2=32$ m.

Displacement $=\sqrt{800^2+32^2}=800.6$ m (B).

questions.question: Two parallel wires are brought close to each other. Wire X has a current of $4$ A flowing through it and wire Y has a current of $6$ A flowing through it. Both currents are flowing in the same direction. From the information we can conclude that:
questions.answer: By Newton's third law the forces on the two wires are equal in magnitude, $\frac FL=\frac{\mu_0I_XI_Y}{2\pi d}$. Parallel currents in the same direction attract, so the force on X is directed towards Y (B).
options: the force on wire X is the same magnitude as the force on wire Y and is directed away from wire Y
the force on wire X is the same magnitude as the force on wire Y and is directed towards wire Y
the force on wire X is larger than the force on wire Y and is directed away from wire Y
the force on wire X is smaller than the force on wire Y and is directed towards wire Y

questions.question: Various charged and uncharged particles are sent through a magnetic field (into the page) as shown. Assuming that all the particles enter the field at the same velocity and the magnitude of the charges on the charged particles are the same, the most likely explanation for the paths that the particles take is that:
questions.answer:
Path II is undeflected, so that particle is neutral. For a positive particle moving to the right in a field into the page, $\mathbf F=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ is upward, so path I (curving up) is positive and path III (curving down) is negative.

The radius is $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$. With equal $v$, $|q|$ and $B$, a larger radius means a larger mass. Path I is nearly straight (large $r$), so its particle is more massive than path III's (B).
options: All the particles are positively charged.
Particle path I is positive and more massive than particle path III, which is negative.
Particle path I is positive and less massive than particle path III, which is negative.

questions.question: A proton moves through a magnetic field of strength $2$ T with a velocity of $150$ m s$^{-1}$ as shown (field into the page, velocity perpendicular to the field). The magnitude of the acceleration of the proton is closest to:

Two wires, one carrying a current of $2$ amps and the other carrying a current of $3$ amps, both of length $4$ m, cross each other perpendicularly: that is, they are $90$ degrees to each other. They are separated by a distance of $1$ cm at the point where they cross. The electromagnetic force between the wires is closest to:
questions.answer: The formula $\frac FL=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$ only applies to parallel wires. For perpendicular wires, the magnetic field of one wire at the other wire (crossing at the midpoints) acts either along the second wire (no force, since $\mathbf F=I\mathbf L\times\mathbf B$ with $\mathbf L\parallel\mathbf B$) or perpendicular to it with equal and opposite directions on the two halves, so the forces cancel. The net force is $0$ N (D).

questions.question:
A uniform electric field is set up between two parallel charged plates P and N as shown in the figure. There is a potential difference $V$ between P and N which are distance $d$ apart. The electric field provides a force $F$ on a small plastic sphere, which is carrying a positive charge $q$ and is on the point of moving from P to N. Assume that gravitational effects on the sphere are negligible.

In terms of $V$ and $q$: how much more electrical potential energy has the sphere on P than it has on N?
questions.answer: The potential energy difference is $\Delta U=qV$ (the sphere has $qV$ more energy at P).

questions.question:
A uniform electric field is set up between two parallel charged plates P and N. There is a potential difference $V$ between P and N which are distance $d$ apart. A small plastic sphere carrying a positive charge $q$ is on the point of moving from P to N. Assume that gravitational effects on the sphere are negligible.

In terms of $V$ and $q$: what must be the increase in the kinetic energy of the sphere as it moves from P to N?
questions.answer: All the lost potential energy becomes kinetic energy: $\Delta E_k=qV$.

questions.question:
A uniform electric field is set up between two parallel charged plates P and N. There is a potential difference $V$ between P and N which are distance $d$ apart. A small plastic sphere carrying a positive charge $q$ is on the point of moving from P to N. Assume that gravitational effects on the sphere are negligible.

In terms of $V$ and $q$: how much work is done by the electric field in moving the sphere from P to N?
questions.answer: The work done by the field equals the gain in kinetic energy: $W=qV$.

questions.question:
Two insulated brass plates, P and Q, stand vertically $12$ cm apart, and are connected as shown in the figure to a $720$ V supply. When a small positively charged sphere at the end of an insulating rod is placed as illustrated at the point X, $6.0$ cm from the plate P, the electrical force acting on it is $12$ mN to the left.

Specify fully the electric field strength between the plates.
questions.answer:
$E=\dfrac Vd=\dfrac{720}{0.12}=6000$ V m$^{-1}$ (N C$^{-1}$), uniform between the plates and directed from the positive plate P to the negative plate Q (to the right, as the school's answer gives).

*The question says the force on the positive sphere is to the left, but in the diagram P is positive, so the field, and the force on a positive charge, point to the right. The magnitudes in this question are not affected.*

questions.question:
Two insulated brass plates, P and Q, stand vertically $12$ cm apart, and are connected as shown in the figure to a $720$ V supply. When a small positively charged sphere at the end of an insulating rod is placed as illustrated at the point X, $6.0$ cm from the plate P, the electrical force acting on it is $12$ mN to the left.

What is the charge on the sphere?
questions.answer: $F=Eq\Rightarrow q=\dfrac FE=\dfrac{12\times10^{-3}}{6000}=2\times10^{-6}$ C.

questions.question:
Two insulated brass plates, P and Q, stand vertically $12$ cm apart, and are connected as shown in the figure to a $720$ V supply. When a small positively charged sphere at the end of an insulating rod is placed as illustrated at the point X, $6.0$ cm from the plate P, the electrical force acting on it is $12$ mN to the left.

The separation of the plates is increased to $16$ cm. What is now the magnitude of the electric force on the charged sphere?

Two insulated brass plates, P and Q, stand vertically $12$ cm apart, and are connected as shown in the figure to a $720$ V supply. When a small positively charged sphere at the end of an insulating rod is placed as illustrated at the point X, $6.0$ cm from the plate P, the electrical force acting on it is $12$ mN to the left.

With the plates again $12$ cm apart, the voltage selector on the power supply is adjusted. If the new force on the sphere is $1.6$ mN, what is now the potential difference across the plates?

A current-carrying loop of wire VWXYZ is placed in a magnetic field which is directed to the left, as indicated in the figure.

What is the direction of the magnetic force acting on section WX?
questions.answer: The cell's positive terminal (long plate) is at the top, so conventional current flows $V\to W\to X\to Y\to Z$. In WX the current is downward and the field is to the left. By $\mathbf F=I\mathbf L\times\mathbf B$ (right-hand rule), the force is **into the page**.

questions.question:
A current-carrying loop of wire VWXYZ is placed in a magnetic field which is directed to the left, as indicated in the figure.

What is the direction of the magnetic force acting on section XY?
questions.answer: Current flows from X to Y, i.e. downward and to the left. Only the component perpendicular to the field (the downward part) experiences a force, which for a downward current in a leftward field is **into the page**.

questions.question:
A current-carrying loop of wire VWXYZ is placed in a magnetic field which is directed to the left, as indicated in the figure.

What is the direction of the magnetic force acting on section YZ?
questions.answer: In YZ the current flows to the left, parallel to the field, so $\sin\theta=0$ and the force is **zero**.

questions.question: Two positive charges, identical in mass and charge, enter a uniform electric field. One charge enters the field with no velocity. The other charge enters the field with a velocity that is in the same direction as the field. Mathematically or otherwise, explain why the magnitude of the change in velocity of the moving charge will always be less than the change in velocity of the stationary charge after both have moved through the same distance in the field. In your answer you should compare the work done on both charges for this distance in the field.
questions.answer:
**Work.** The field is uniform, so the force on each charge is the same constant $F=qE$ whatever its speed, and each moves the same distance $s$ along the field. So the work done on each is the same, $W=qEs$ (equivalently $W=qV$ with $V=Es$), and each gains the same kinetic energy.

**Acceleration.** Since $F=qE$ is the same and the masses are the same, $a=\frac{qE}m$ is the same for both.

**Change in velocity.** For the charge starting at rest, $\frac12mv^2=W$, so $\Delta v=\sqrt{2W/m}$. For the moving charge with initial speed $u$:
$$\frac12mv^2-\frac12mu^2=W\Rightarrow\Delta v=v-u=\frac{2W}{m(v+u)}.$$
Since $u>0$ the denominator is larger than for the charge starting at rest (where it is $mv$), so $\Delta v$ is smaller. (Equivalently, the moving charge covers the distance in less time, so the same acceleration acts for a shorter time and produces a smaller change in velocity.)

questions.question:
A stream of positive ions each carrying a charge $q$ travels vertically downwards between two charged, vertical plates between which the electric field strength is $2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ towards the west. A magnetic field at right angles to the electric field and of flux density $4.0$ mT between the plates keeps the beam travelling in a straight line.

What is the net force on each ion due to the electric and magnetic fields?
questions.answer: The ions travel in a straight line at constant velocity, so the net force is **zero** (the electric and magnetic forces are equal and opposite).

questions.question:
A stream of positive ions each carrying a charge $q$ travels vertically downwards between two charged, vertical plates between which the electric field strength is $2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ towards the west. A magnetic field at right angles to the electric field and of flux density $4.0$ mT between the plates keeps the beam travelling in a straight line.

What must be the direction of the magnetic field?
questions.answer: The electric force on a positive ion is to the west, so the magnetic force must be to the east. Using $\mathbf F=q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ with $\mathbf v$ downward and $\mathbf F$ to the east, the right-hand rule gives $\mathbf B$ **to the north**.

questions.question:
A stream of positive ions each carrying a charge $q$ travels vertically downwards between two charged, vertical plates between which the electric field strength is $2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ towards the west. A magnetic field at right angles to the electric field and of flux density $4.0$ mT between the plates keeps the beam travelling in a straight line.

In terms of $q$, specify fully the electric force acting on each ion.
questions.answer: $F=qE=2.0\times10^4q$ newtons, directed to the west.

questions.question:
A stream of positive ions each carrying a charge $q$ travels vertically downwards between two charged, vertical plates between which the electric field strength is $2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ towards the west. A magnetic field at right angles to the electric field and of flux density $4.0$ mT between the plates keeps the beam travelling in a straight line.

In terms of $q$ and $v$, the speed of the ions, specify fully the magnetic force on each ion.
questions.answer: $F=qvB=4.0\times10^{-3}qv$ newtons, directed to the east (opposite to the electric force).

questions.question:
A stream of positive ions each carrying a charge $q$ travels vertically downwards between two charged, vertical plates between which the electric field strength is $2.0\times10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ towards the west. A magnetic field at right angles to the electric field and of flux density $4.0$ mT between the plates keeps the beam travelling in a straight line.

Deduce the value for the speed $v$.
questions.answer: For no deflection $qvB=qE$, so $v=\dfrac EB=\dfrac{2.0\times10^4}{4.0\times10^{-3}}=5.0\times10^6$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
In an experiment, two $50$ cm long sections of wire are mounted parallel to each other. They exert a repulsive force of $4\times10^{-6}$ N on each other when they each carry a current of $5$ A.

How far apart are the wires spaced?
questions.answer: $F=\dfrac{\mu_0}{2\pi}\dfrac{I_1I_2l}{d}\Rightarrow d=\dfrac{(2\times10^{-7})(5)(5)(0.5)}{4\times10^{-6}}=0.625$ m.

questions.question:
In an experiment, two $50$ cm long sections of wire are mounted parallel to each other. They exert a repulsive force of $4\times10^{-6}$ N on each other when they each carry a current of $5$ A.

Are the currents in the wires in the same or opposite directions?
questions.answer: **Opposite** directions: parallel wires repel when the currents are in opposite directions.

questions.question: Using the formula for the force on a charge $q$ moving through a magnetic field $B$ with a velocity $v$, and simple kinematics and circuit theory, derive an expression for the force on a wire of length $l$ carrying a current $I$ in a magnetic field $B$. Show all the steps involved in your derivation.
questions.answer:
A charge $q$ moving at velocity $v$ at angle $\theta$ to the field experiences $F=qvB\sin\theta$.

Consider charge $q$ moving along a length $l$ of wire in time $t$, so $v=\dfrac lt$. Then
$$F=q\frac ltB\sin\theta=\frac qt\,lB\sin\theta.$$
Since current is the charge passing per unit time, $I=\dfrac qt$, so
$$F=BIl\sin\theta.$$

questions.question: Using the relationship between magnetic force and the resulting centripetal force that occurs when a charged particle moves perpendicularly through a uniform magnetic field, and for circular motion kinematics, $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}{T}$, show mathematically or otherwise that the period of rotation of the particle through the field is independent of its speed through the magnetic field.
questions.answer:
The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}r$, so $qB=\dfrac{mv}r$.

Substituting $v=\dfrac{2\pi r}T$: $qB=\dfrac{m}{r}\cdot\dfrac{2\pi r}T=\dfrac{2\pi m}T$, so
$$T=\frac{2\pi m}{qB}.$$
The period depends only on $m$, $q$ and $B$, and $v$ (and $r$) cancel, so it is independent of speed.

questions.question: An electron is fired into a region of space where an electric field and a magnetic field are present. In the space below, sketch the orientation of these two fields if the electron is to pass through the region undeflected. (Ignore gravitational effects.)
questions.answer:
For no deflection the electric and magnetic forces on the electron must be equal and opposite, which needs $E=vB$ with the fields perpendicular to each other and to the velocity.

One arrangement (sketched): the electron moves to the right, $\mathbf B$ points into the page, and $\mathbf E$ points downward (top plate positive, bottom plate negative). The electric force on the electron is upward (opposite to $\mathbf E$) and the magnetic force $-e\,\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ is downward, so they can cancel.

Another valid answer: $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ both parallel (or antiparallel) to the electron's velocity. Then $\mathbf v\times\mathbf B=\mathbf 0$ so there is no magnetic force, and the electric force acts along the line of motion, so the electron is not deflected (it only speeds up or slows down).",answer_images=[f"{IMG}/a19.png"])
